_articles: Latin has no words for 'a' or 'the': the same noun can be 'a girl', 'the girl' or just 'girl' — English adds whichever the sentence needs.

_enclitics.que: -que is glued to the end of a word and means 'and', joining that word to what came before: 'senātus populusque' = the senate and the people.
_enclitics.ne: -ne is glued to the first word of a sentence to turn it into a yes/no question: 'Fābulamne vīs?' = Do you want a story? It expects no particular answer (compare nōnne, num).
_enclitics.ve: -ve is glued to the end of a word and means 'or': 'bis terve' = twice or three times.

cases.abl: from, away from; by (the person doing a passive verb)

a.usage: Takes the ablative. 'ā' before consonants, 'ab' before vowels and h. With a passive verb it marks the agent: 'ā Daedalō aedificātus' = built by Daedalus.

ab.usage: Takes the ablative. 'ab' before vowels and h, 'ā' before consonants. With a passive verb it marks the agent: 'ab Athēniēnsibus' = by the Athenians.

abs.usage: Takes the ablative; a rare form of ab used before t.

e.usage: Takes the ablative. 'ē' before consonants, 'ex' before vowels (and often consonants too): 'ex urbe' = out of the city.

ex.usage: Takes the ablative: 'ex urbe Athēnīs' = from the city of Athens.

de.usage: Takes the ablative. Most often 'about': 'fābula dē lupō' = a story about the wolf.

cum.usage: As a preposition it takes the ablative: 'cum cēterīs' = with the others; it is glued onto pronouns: mēcum, tēcum, sēcum, quōcum. As a conjunction (with a verb, no noun after it) it means 'when' (indicative) or 'when / since / although' (subjunctive).

sine.usage: Takes the ablative: 'sine fīlō' = without a thread.

cases.abl: in front of; on behalf of, for; instead of

pro.usage: Takes the ablative: 'prō patriā' = for one's country.

cases.abl: before, in front of; because of

in.usage: Two cases, two meanings. Ablative = where something is: 'in labyrinthō habitābat' = he lived in the labyrinth. Accusative = where something goes: 'in labyrinthum dūcī' = to be led into the labyrinth.

sub.usage: Ablative for position under something, accusative for motion under it.

ad.usage: Takes the accusative: 'ad mortem certam' = to certain death; 'ad nāvigandum' = for sailing.

cases.acc: through, across; during; by means of

per.usage: Takes the accusative: 'per caelum' = across the sky.

post.usage: Takes the accusative: 'post currum' = behind the chariot. Also an adverb: 'afterwards'.

ante.usage: Takes the accusative. Also an adverb: 'paucīs annīs ante' = a few years before.

cases.acc: at, near; at the house of; among

circum.usage: Takes the accusative: 'circum moenia' = around the walls.

ob.usage: Takes the accusative: 'quam ob rem' = for what reason, why.

usque.usage: 'all the way': 'ūsque ad' = right up to.

prope.usage: Takes the accusative. Also an adverb: 'nearly'.

causa.usage: Ablative of causa placed after a genitive: 'glōriae causā' = for the sake of glory.

gratia.usage: Placed after a genitive: 'exemplī grātiā' = for the sake of example.

et.usage: 'and'. Doubled, 'et … et' = both … and. Before a single word it can mean 'even, also'.

que.usage: Enclitic 'and': glued to the second of the two things joined: 'adulēscentēs virginēsque' = young men and maidens.

atque.usage: 'and also, and what is more' — a stronger 'and'. 'ac' before consonants. After words of likeness: 'īdem atque' = the same as.

ac.usage: 'and, and also' (form of atque used before consonants).

neque.usage: 'and not, nor'. 'neque … neque' = neither … nor. Latin says 'and not' where English says 'and … not'.

aut.usage: 'or' between real alternatives. 'aut … aut' = either … or.

vel.usage: 'or' (if you like — the choice does not matter). Before an adjective: 'even'.

ve.usage: Enclitic 'or', glued to a word: 'bis terve' = twice or three times.

sed.usage: 'but'. 'nōn modo … sed etiam' = not only … but also.

at.usage: 'but, yet' — a sharper objection than sed, often starting a reply: 'At tāle mōnstrum tē terrēbit' = But such a monster will frighten you.

autem.usage: 'but, however, on the other hand' — a mild contrast. Never first in its sentence (postpositive).

vero.usage: 'in truth, indeed'; as a connector 'but, however'. Comes second in its sentence: 'Iam vērō … cupiō'.

nam.usage: 'for' (giving the reason for what was just said), starts its sentence.

enim.usage: 'for' (giving a reason); always second in its sentence: 'Rēx enim … male volēbat' = for the king wished ill.

igitur.usage: 'therefore, so'; usually second in its sentence.

quia.usage: 'because' (with the indicative for a plain fact).

quod.usage: As a conjunction: 'because' (also 'the fact that'). Also the neuter of quī: 'which, that'. If a verb follows and no noun agrees with it, read 'because'.

ut.usage: With the indicative: 'as, when, how'. With the subjunctive: 'so that, in order that' (purpose or result) or 'that' after verbs of ordering, asking, wishing (imperat ut … = orders that …). The negative of the subjunctive uses is nē (ut nōn for result).

ne.usage: With the subjunctive: 'that … not, lest' — the negative of ut in commands and purposes: 'imperat nē abeant' = orders them not to leave. 'nē + imperative' (nē timē!) or nōlī + infinitive = don't. Not to be confused with the enclitic -ne, which asks a question.

si.usage: 'if'. Indicative for open conditions; subjunctive for imagined or impossible ones ('if he were …').

dum.usage: 'while' (present indicative, even about the past); 'until' (subjunctive when waiting for something); 'provided that' (dummodo).

postquam.usage: 'after' + a verb, normally in the perfect indicative: 'postquam nārrāvit' = after she told.

antequam.usage: 'before' + a verb. Indicative for a fact; subjunctive when the action was anticipated or prevented.

etsi.usage: 'even if, although': 'etsī iānua patet' = even though the door stands open.

an.usage: 'or' in questions: 'Fābulamne dē lupō … an fābulam dē puerō?' = a story about the wolf, or one about the boy? Alone, it opens a surprised question: 'An cupis …?' = Or do you want …? In indirect questions: 'whether'.

num.usage: Asks a question expecting the answer 'no': 'Num timēs?' = You're not afraid, are you? In indirect questions: 'whether'.

nonne.usage: Asks a question expecting the answer 'yes': 'Nōnne vidēs?' = Surely you see? / Don't you see?

quin.usage: 'that not, from … -ing' after verbs of doubting or preventing (+ subjunctive); 'why not? indeed'.

licet.usage: As a conjunction: 'although' (+ subjunctive). As a verb: 'it is allowed'.

modo.usage: 'only, just; just now'. 'nōn modo … sed etiam' = not only … but also. 'modo … modo' = now … now.

non.usage: 'not'. Goes right before the word it denies. Latin has no 'do not': 'nōn videt' = he does not see.

ne_adv.usage: 'not' in commands and wishes: 'nē timē!'. Also 'nē … quidem' = not even.

haud.usage: 'not at all, by no means' — stronger than nōn, usually with an adjective or adverb.

iam.usage: 'now, already; by now'. With a negative: 'iam nōn' = no longer.

tunc.usage: 'then, at that time': 'quī tunc Crētam regēbat' = who was then ruling Crete.

hic_adv.usage: 'here' (adverb, long ī) — not the pronoun hic 'this'.

illuc.usage: 'to there, thither': 'illūc vehēbantur' = were carried there.

quo.usage: 'to where, whither'. Also the ablative of quī: 'by which, in which'.

quam.usage: 'how' (in exclamations and questions: 'Quam fābulam?' = what story?); 'than' after a comparative; 'as … as possible' with a superlative (quam celerrimē).

tam.usage: 'so' (with an adjective or adverb): 'tam fortis' = so brave. 'tam … quam' = as … as.

ita.usage: 'so, thus, in this way'; as an answer, 'yes'.

sic.usage: 'thus, in this way, like this': 'sīc nārrāre incipit' = begins to tell like this.

quoque.usage: 'also, too'. Stands right after the word it stresses: 'Mīnōtaurum ipsum quoque' = the Minotaur himself too.

etiam.usage: 'also, even; still'. 'nōn modo … sed etiam' = not only … but also.

quidem.usage: 'indeed, at least' — stresses the word before it. 'nē … quidem' = not even.

olim.usage: 'once upon a time, formerly; one day (in the future)'.

solum.usage: 'only'. 'nōn sōlum … sed etiam' = not only … but also.

magis.usage: 'more, rather' (comparative of much): 'magis … quam' = more … than.

male.usage: 'badly'. 'male velle' + dative = to wish someone ill.

primum.usage: 'first, at first'. 'quam prīmum' = as soon as possible.

forte.usage: 'by chance': 'quī forte … vēnērunt' = who happened to come. Not the adjective fortis.

paulo.usage: 'a little' (ablative of degree with comparatives and ante/post): 'paulō ante' = a little before.

o.usage: 'O!' — goes with a vocative when calling someone: 'ō Quīnte!'

utinam.usage: 'if only! would that!' — introduces a wish with the subjunctive: 'utinam venīret' = if only he would come.

is.usage: 'he, she, it, they' when standing alone; 'that, this' with a noun. Its genitive eius = 'his, her, its' (someone else's; for the subject's own use suus). Often the plain English 'the': 'eō colōre' = by that colour.

hic.usage: 'this' (near me, the speaker). Standing alone: 'this man/woman/thing', 'he/she/it'.

ille.usage: 'that' (over there, away from both of us); also 'the famous', or 'the former' vs hic 'the latter'. Standing alone: 'he, she, it'.

iste.usage: 'that (of yours)', often with a sneer: 'istās fābulās' = those stories of yours.

ipse.usage: '-self' for emphasis: 'Mīnōtaurum ipsum' = the Minotaur himself. Not reflexive — that is sē.

idem.usage: 'the same': 'ad eundem rīvum' = to the same stream. is + -dem.

qui.usage: Relative 'who, which, that': its gender and number come from the noun it refers to, its case from its job in its own clause. At the start of a sentence it links back like 'he, this': 'Quī iam antequam …' = He, already before …

quis.usage: 'who? what?' After sī, nisi, num, nē it means 'anyone, anything'.

ego.usage: 'I'. Latin verbs already say who acts, so ego appears only for stress or contrast.

tu.usage: 'you' (one person). Used for stress: 'Tē hīc manēre volō' = I want YOU to stay here.

nos.usage: 'we, us'. Genitive nostrum (of us, partitive) / nostrī (objective).

se.usage: 'himself, herself, itself, themselves' — refers back to the subject of its clause (or of the main verb in reported speech). No nominative. sēcum = with himself.

suus.usage: 'his / her / its / their OWN' — belonging to the subject. For someone else's, Latin uses eius / eōrum: 'post currum suum' = behind his own chariot, 'corpus eius' = his (Hector's) body.

aliquis.usage: 'someone, something; some': 'aliquam fābulam' = some story. Declines like quis with ali- in front.

quidam.usage: 'a certain (one), some' — known to the speaker but not named. Declines like quī + -dam (quendam, quandam).

nemo.usage: 'no one, nobody'. Latin uses one negative where English uses 'not … anyone'.

uterque.usage: 'each of two, both' (with a singular verb).

alter.usage: 'the other (of two); the second'. 'alter … alter' = the one … the other.

totus.usage: 'whole, entire'. Genitive tōtīus, dative tōtī (like ūnus).

talis.usage: 'such, of such a kind': 'tālem fābulam' = such a story. 'tālis … quālis' = such … as.

tantus.usage: 'so great, so much'. 'tantus … quantus' = as great … as.

quantus.usage: 'how great? how much?; as great as'.

unus.usage: 'one; only, alone'. Genitive ūnīus, dative ūnī. The ablative ūnā is also an adverb: 'ūnā cum' = together with.

sum.usage: 'be'. With a dative it shows possession: 'cui caput taurī erat' = who had a bull's head (literally: to whom there was …). Often left out in Latin where English needs 'is'.

inquam.usage: 'I say / he says / he said' — used only inside or after a direct quotation, never before it: 'Nōlī' inquit 'mē relinquere!'
